title: Sample space, events and the three rules every probability obeys

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A chance process is anything whose result is not known until it runs: a roll of a die, a man picked at random from a list. An outcome is one result it can give. The sample space is the complete list of outcomes, the term of Book 0, D1. An event is any set of outcomes taken from the sample space.

From two events A and B, three more are built.

  • “A and B” is the set of outcomes that are in both A and B.
  • “A or B” is the set of outcomes in at least one of them. Outcomes in both are included.
  • “Not A”, the complement of A, is every outcome in the sample space that is outside A.

A Venn diagram draws these. A box stands for the sample space and a circle for each event. The overlap of two circles is “A and B”. Everything inside either circle is “A or B”.

P(A), read “the probability of A”, is a number given to the event A. Every probability obeys three rules.

  1. No probability is negative: P(A) is 0 or more, for every event A.
  2. The whole sample space has probability 1.
  3. If A and B are mutually exclusive, so that no outcome is in both, then P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

First, the complement. A and not A are mutually exclusive, and together they make up the whole sample space.

P(A) + P(not A) = P(A or not A)    by rule 3
P(A or not A) = 1    by rule 2
so P(not A) = 1 − P(A)

Second, the general addition rule, for any two events, mutually exclusive or not. Cut “A or B” into three pieces that share no outcome: “A and not B”, “A and B”, and “B and not A”. Rule 3, used twice, adds them. For any number of pieces that share no outcome, add them.

P(A or B) = P(A and not B) + P(A and B) + P(B and not A)
P(A) = P(A and not B) + P(A and B)
P(B) = P(B and not A) + P(A and B)
P(A) + P(B) = P(A and not B) + P(B and not A) + 2 × P(A and B)
P(A) + P(B) = P(A or B) + P(A and B)
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

When A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A and B) is 0, and rule 3 comes back.

The overlap P(A and B) is at least 0. It is at most the smaller of P(A) and P(B). Put each limit into the rule. With no overlap, P(A or B) is P(A) + P(B), its largest. When one event sits inside the other, P(A or B) is the larger of the two, its smallest. It can never pass 1.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Write down everything that could happen. That list is the sample space. Any group of items on it is an event.

Two events that can both happen need one more step. Adding them counts the overlap twice, so you take the overlap away once.

blocks.alt: Four bars from zero: flagged only 23, both 36, in the band only 6, neither 66. Together they make 131.
blocks.caption: The 131 men of Kiran’s rebuilt table (Illustration 1), cut into the four pieces a Venn diagram of “flagged by the arm tape” and “in the 25-29.9 band” makes. No circles are drawn here: each bar is one piece, and its height is the number of men in it: 23 flagged only, 36 both, 6 in the band only, 66 neither. “Flagged or in the band” is the first three pieces, 65 men. Adding the flagged 59 and the band’s 42 gives 101, because the 36 men in both are counted twice.

blocks.alt: Five bars from zero: P(A) 0.4504, P(B) 0.3206, P(A and B) 0.2748, P(A) + P(B) 0.7710, P(A or B) 0.4962.
blocks.caption: Pick one of the 131 men at random; A is “flagged” and B is “in the band”. Adding P(A), 0.4504, and P(B), 0.3206, gives 0.7710, which counts the 36 men in both twice. Taking P(A and B), 0.2748, away once gives P(A or B), 0.4962: the 65 men of the call list divided by 131.

blocks.alt: Three bars from zero: 0.3333 for diabetes, 0.75 for no diabetes, and 1.0833 for the two added, above a dashed line at 1.
blocks.caption: The physician’s two made-up beliefs about one man: one in three that he has diabetes, three in four that he has not. The two events are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility, so the rules require them to add to 1. They add to 1.0833, so both cannot be right.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Book 0 rebuilt a table from Kiran and colleagues’ study of medical students in Mangaluru (Book 0, D3). It covers 131 men. The tape flags a man when his upper arm measures 31.3 centimetres or more. “In the band” means a body-mass index from 25 to 29.9. The table is rebuilt from the paper’s printed percentages, not printed by the paper in this form.

in the band not in the band total
arm 31.3 cm or more 36 23 59
arm under 31.3 cm 6 66 72
total 42 89 131

A camp organiser wants to call back every man the tape flags, and every man in the band. How many men is that? The move you reach for first is to add the row and the column.

59 plus 42 = 101

That is 101 men, and it is wrong. Look at the 36 men who are flagged and in the band. They sit in the flagged row and in the band column. Adding the row and the column counted each of them twice.

Picture a Venn diagram. The box is the 131 men. One circle is “flagged”, the other is “in the band”. The circles cut the box into four pieces that share no man. The first figure draws the four pieces as bars.

59 minus 36 = 23
42 minus 36 = 6
23 plus 36 plus 6 = 65
131 minus 65 = 66

So 23 men are flagged only, 36 are both, 6 are in the band only, and 66 are neither. The call list is the first three pieces: 65 men.

Now do it with probabilities. Pick one of the 131 men at random. Each man has the same chance, so the probability of an event is its count divided by 131. Call “flagged” A and “in the band” B. Use the general addition rule. These divisions do not come out exactly, so each is rounded to four decimal places, and the sign ≈, read “is about”, marks a rounded result.

59 divided by 131 ≈ 0.4504
42 divided by 131 ≈ 0.3206
36 divided by 131 ≈ 0.2748
0.4504 plus 0.3206 minus 0.2748 = 0.4962
65 divided by 131 ≈ 0.4962

P(A or B) is 0.4962, and counting the 65 men directly gives the same. The 101 men of the first try would have given 0.7710, which is 101 divided by 131.

The complement rule finds the men left off the list.

1 minus 0.4962 = 0.5038
66 divided by 131 ≈ 0.5038

About half the men, 66 of 131, are neither flagged nor in the band.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The counts are the rebuilt table of Book 0, D3, worked back from the paper’s rounded percentages. They hold for these 131 men, students at one college. “In the band” leaves out the 10 men with an index of 30 or more, so “not in the band” is not the same as “a normal index”.

Turning counts into probabilities by dividing by 131 needs every man to have the same chance of being picked. The rules themselves do not need that. They hold however the probabilities were set.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
The same rules bind a probability that is a belief rather than a count. Suppose a physician looks at a man in clinic, before any test. She says: “I’d put his chance of diabetes at one in three. And I’d put his chance of not having it at three in four.” Check her two numbers against the rules. Being diabetic and not being diabetic are mutually exclusive, and together they cover every possibility. So the two must add to 1.

1 divided by 3 ≈ 0.3333
3 divided by 4 = 0.75
0.3333 plus 0.75 = 1.0833

They add to more than 1. The rules cannot say which number is wrong. They say both cannot be right. If she stands by one in three, the other must be two in three.

1 minus 0.3333 = 0.6667

Grinstead and Snell describe this kind of probability in Introduction to Probability (https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf), §1.2: “you can determine your own personal probability by seeing what kind of a bet you would be willing to make.” Price her beliefs as bets. At one in three, a ticket that pays 1 rupee if he has diabetes is worth a third of a rupee to her. At three in four, a ticket that pays 1 rupee if he has not is worth three-quarters of a rupee. Buying both costs her 1.0833 rupees. Whatever is true, exactly one ticket pays, and it pays 1 rupee.

0.3333 plus 0.75 minus 1 = 0.0833

She loses 0.0833 rupees for certain. That is what breaking the rules costs.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The physician and her numbers are made up. The check shows only that two beliefs contradict each other. A belief that passes every rule can still be badly wrong about this man. The rules test how numbers fit together, never whether any one of them matches the world.

points.html: Before you add, ask whether one person can be in both groups. If yes, subtract the overlap once.
In this book “A or B” means at least one, both included.

When two percentages are reported and their overlap is not, P(A or B) is known only as a range. It is at least the larger of the two. It is at most their sum, and never above 1. The same holds for three or more groups: at least the largest, at most the sum. Quote the range, not the sum.
The shares of categories that cannot overlap must add to 100 per cent.
The three rules check that probabilities fit together. They cannot check that any one probability is true.
Before you subtract an overlap, check that both percentages share one denominator.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “P(A or B) is P(A) plus P(B).” That is rule 3, and it holds only when A and B cannot both happen. For events that can overlap it counts the overlap twice. Kiran’s flagged row and band column add to 101 men when only 65 are on the call list: the 36 men in both were counted twice.

blocks.prompt: From memory: state the three rules every probability obeys. Then write the general addition rule, and say in one sentence why the last term is subtracted.
blocks.answer:
No probability is negative. The whole sample space has probability 1. If two events cannot both happen, the probability of one or the other is the sum of their probabilities.

The general addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

The outcomes in both A and B are counted once in P(A) and again in P(B). Subtracting P(A and B) takes the second count away, so each outcome is counted once.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up survey of 400 clinic attenders asks “Which of these do you have?” and lets each person tick as many as apply. The report prints:

condition share ticking it (%)
diabetes 30
hypertension 45
overweight 40

A committee member adds the three and says “115 per cent: so everyone has at least one, and some have two.” Say what the table does and does not show.
blocks.answer:
The three shares add to 115 per cent.

30 plus 45 plus 40 = 115

A list of categories that cannot overlap must add to 100 per cent. This one adds to more, which tells you the categories overlap: people ticked more than one. The table even forces a count. The 400 people made 460 ticks, so there are at least 60 ticks beyond one each. One person can carry at most two extra ticks.

1.15 times 400 = 460
460 minus 400 = 60
60 divided by 2 = 30

So at least 30 people ticked more than one. That much the table shows.

It does not show that everyone has at least one. The share with at least one is “diabetes or hypertension or overweight”. Without the overlaps it is known only as a range. It is at least 45 per cent, the largest single share, if everyone with diabetes or overweight also has hypertension. It is at most 100 per cent. The 115 is not a count of anything: people with two conditions are in it twice and people with three are in it three times.

To get the share with at least one, the survey must report how many ticked none. Then the complement rule gives it: 1 minus the share with none.

blocks.prompt:
A fair die is rolled once. Its sample space is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, each equally likely. Event A is “an even number”. Event B is “4 or more”.

List the outcomes in A, in B, in “A and B”, in “A or B” and in “not A”.
blocks.answer:
A is 2, 4 and 6. B is 4, 5 and 6.

“A and B” is the outcomes in both: 4 and 6.

“A or B” is the outcomes in at least one: 2, 4, 5 and 6. The 4 and the 6 are listed once.

“Not A” is the outcomes outside A: 1, 3 and 5.

blocks.prompt: P(A) is 0.3, P(B) is 0.5 and P(A and B) is 0.1. Work out P(A or B), and the probability that neither A nor B happens.
blocks.answer:
Use the general addition rule.

0.3 plus 0.5 minus 0.1 = 0.7

P(A or B) is 0.7. “Neither A nor B” is the complement of “A or B”.

1 minus 0.7 = 0.3

The probability that neither happens is 0.3.

blocks.prompt: P(A) is 0.45, P(B) is 0.30 and P(A or B) is 0.60. Work out P(A and B). Are A and B mutually exclusive?
blocks.answer:
Turn the general addition rule round. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B), so P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A or B).

0.45 plus 0.30 = 0.75
0.75 minus 0.60 = 0.15

P(A and B) is 0.15. It is above zero, so some outcomes are in both. A and B are not mutually exclusive.

blocks.prompt:
Kiran and colleagues’ Table 2 sorts the 131 men by body-mass index (BMI, weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres). It gives 5 men below 18.5, 74 from 18.5 to 24.9, 42 from 25 to 29.9 and 10 at 30 or more.

Pick one of the 131 men at random. Work out the probability that his BMI is 25 or more, and the probability that it is 18.5 or more. Say which rule you used each time.
blocks.answer:
The four bands cannot overlap: each man has one BMI. Check that they cover all 131 men.

5 plus 74 plus 42 plus 10 = 131

“25 or more” is “25 to 29.9 or 30 and over”, two mutually exclusive bands. Rule 3 adds them.

42 divided by 131 ≈ 0.3206
10 divided by 131 ≈ 0.0763
0.3206 plus 0.0763 = 0.3969
52 divided by 131 ≈ 0.3969

The probability is 0.3969: 52 of the 131 men.

“18.5 or more” is the complement of “below 18.5”. The complement rule is quickest.

5 divided by 131 ≈ 0.0382
1 minus 0.0382 = 0.9618

The probability is 0.9618: 126 of the 131 men.

blocks.prompt:
Take the same 131 men. Kiran’s Table 2 gives 52 with a BMI of 25 or more. It gives 41 with a waist of 90 cm or more. The paper does not say how many men are in both groups.

Pick one man at random. Between what limits must the probability lie that he has a BMI of 25 or more or a waist of 90 cm or more? Say when each limit would be reached.
blocks.answer:
The general addition rule needs the overlap, which is missing. So work out the two extremes.

The most the overlap can be is 41, if every man with the large waist also has the high BMI. Then “either” is only the 52.

52 minus 41 = 11
52 divided by 131 ≈ 0.3969

The least the overlap can be is 0, if no man is in both. Then “either” is every man in either group.

52 plus 41 = 93
93 divided by 131 ≈ 0.7099

The probability lies between 0.3969 and 0.7099: between 52 and 93 of the 131 men. In the first case, 11 of the 52 men with the high BMI have a smaller waist. To narrow the range you need the count of men in both groups.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

Kiran’s rebuilt table: 131 men, 59 flagged by the arm tape, 42 in the 25-29.9 band
P(flagged or in the band) = P(flagged) + P(in the band)
= 59 divided by 131 plus 42 divided by 131
= 0.4504 plus 0.3206 = 0.7710
so about 77 per cent of the men are flagged or in the band
blocks.answer:
The second line broke. It adds as if “flagged” and “in the band” could not both happen. They can: 36 men are both. Subtract the overlap once.

36 divided by 131 ≈ 0.2748
0.4504 plus 0.3206 minus 0.2748 = 0.4962

About 50 per cent, 65 men, not 77 per cent.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: “or means add” is the rule Book 0 taught for mutually exclusive events, and the arithmetic in each line is right. The working never asked whether a man could be in both groups.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

A and B cannot both happen. P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.3.
P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B) = 0.2 times 0.3 = 0.06
P(A or B) = 0.2 plus 0.3 minus 0.06 = 0.44
blocks.answer:
The second line broke. A and B cannot both happen, so “A and B” holds no outcome and P(A and B) is 0, not 0.06. Multiplying the two probabilities gives P(A and B) only for independent events, and these are not independent: learning that B happened tells you A did not.

0.2 plus 0.3 minus 0 = 0.5

P(A or B) is 0.5.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: the general addition rule is used correctly, and “multiply for and” is a rule the reader knows from Book 0. It was used where its condition fails.

blocks.prompt:
The NFHS-5 India fact sheet (2019-21) gives two figures for women aged 15-49. In all, 24.0% have overweight or obesity (indicator 88). And 57.0% are anaemic (indicator 95). A district presentation says: “So 81 per cent of women have one problem or the other.”

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what the presentation’s number does not establish.
blocks.answer:
“One or the other” is P(overweight or obese, or anaemic). The general addition rule needs the share of women with both, and the fact sheet does not give it. So compute the range.

24.0 plus 57.0 = 81.0

The 81.0 per cent is the most it could be. It is reached only if no woman with overweight or obesity is also anaemic. The least it could be is 57.0 per cent, if every woman with overweight or obesity is also anaemic. So the share is somewhere from 57.0 to 81.0 per cent, and the presentation quoted the top of the range as the answer.

There is a second problem. The two figures are not shares of the same women. The fact sheet’s footnote 21, on indicator 88, says it “Excludes pregnant women and women with a birth in the preceding 2 months.” Indicator 95 is for all women aged 15-49. Before combining them at all, say that the two groups differ.

What the numbers do not establish: how many women have both, and so how many have at least one. Nor do they say that the two conditions are linked or unlinked. A survey table of the two together would answer both questions.
